There's a Serious Problem With How Heart Symptoms Are Treated in Women, Study Reveals[3]
sections.title: Treating Heart Disease in Women

sections.text: All right, Cara, tell us about treating heart disease in women.
Yeah, not going so well, apparently, unfortunately.
So we talk a lot about equity in health care, not just in outcomes, but also in health care services.
And I think this article that I came across recently really speaks to that.
So it's a write up of a study that was published in the Medical Journal of Australia called Sex Differences in the Management and Outcomes of Non-ST Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes.
And I think it requires a tiny bit of background before I tell you the outcomes of their study.
There's a lot of terminology that gets thrown around.
I had to sort of make sense of a lot of this because I know I had heard a lot of these terms that I hadn't really thought deeply about what they mean.
But commonly we hear the term heart attack, right?
We know of when somebody has a heart attack, but what exactly is a heart attack?
The technical term that's used to describe heart attack is a myocardial infarction.
And infarction, of course, refers to the death of tissue.
Specifically here we're talking about the heart muscle, myo, that's where the myocardial comes from.
Myocardial tissue doesn't get enough oxygen for a variety of reasons, and there's tissue death.

And the larger sort of bucket, because I think that this is going to be necessary to know when we describe the difference between a STEMI and an NSTEMI, the larger bucket is something called acute coronary syndrome.
And that includes a lot of things.
It includes unstable angina.
It includes myocardial infarction, otherwise known as a heart attack.
And within my myocardial infarction, there are two big types that are often described.
There's a STEMI and an NSTEMI.
So STEMI is an ST elevation myocardial infarction.
What that means is that when you look at an EKG, you know, the little wiggles on the screen based on the leads that are placed on the chest, you see that the ST portion of that EKG wave is elevated.
And an NSTEMI, which stands for non, that's where the N comes in, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, you actually don't see that elevation.
Now sometimes you see other changes to the EKG.
That's neither here nor there, but you might see an ST depression, you might see a T inversion.
But the big takeaway is that sometimes it doesn't look like an abnormal EKG at all.
Sometimes you can't diagnose a heart attack just on the EKG.
You can diagnose a STEMI heart attack, a STEMI myocardial infarction, but not an NSTEMI.
You actually then also, which is standard now, is you have to look at a blood test to see if there are markers of heart damage.
One of the big ones is troponin that's released when the heart muscle itself actually starts to die.
So you can see the heart, you can see those factors in the blood, which is why it's very important that both pieces of evidence are taken together.
Generally speaking, STEMIs can be kind of classified as more severe, but let's be clear here.
NSTEMIs are also very, very severe.
They can be very damaging.
And a lot of it has to do downstream with either total, like complete blockage of an artery or partial blockage of an artery.

So all of that background is necessary to understand what happened in this study, where the researchers looked at a big registry of acute coronary care that was in Australia across 43 Australian hospitals across about a decade.
And they specifically were looking at people with NSTEMI, so non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
And they, I think it ended up being, yeah, something like 7,783 patients.
Only 2,422 of them were women.
So right there you see a big difference off the bat.
Women just by and large had fewer cases of this type of heart attack.
And that follows across the board.
Even though heart attack is a common cause of death in women, even though it is a high risk factor, it's still, when you compare genders, is not as frequent as in men.
But within that, they started to kind of look at a lot of demographic information, which they always do in these studies.
But the main outcome measures were, what did the physicians do after somebody came in with an NSTEMI?
And they looked at both the immediate outcome, like what happened upon discharge, and then a six-month follow-up outcome.
And here is what they found.
They found that fewer women underwent cardiac catheterization.
They found that women had a longer median time to get that catheterization.
They found that fewer women were prescribed aspirin.
They found that fewer women were given antiplatelet medications other than aspirin.
Fewer women were prescribed beta blockers.
Fewer women were prescribed statins.
And fewer women, and this is a really big difference, were referred to cardiac rehab, a difference of 54% to 63%.
They found that fewer women underwent that bypass grafting.
Again fewer women, so this is within a different group.
This is coronary artery disease as a whole, so not just the NSTEMI women, but women who also had, or sorry, women and men who also had unstable angina.
Fewer women in that group underwent CABG.
Fewer women were given statins.
Fewer women were also referred for cardiac rehabilitation.

Yeah, so across the board, basically the overall outcomes were the women in this study received less evidence-based treatment than the men, consistent with, and this was consistent with studies that were done before.

So even though they were just specifically looking in Australia, they referenced a lot of literature from around the world that showed that by and large women in these, women are receiving less evidence-based treatment when they come in for heart attack than men.
This study specifically looked at NSTEMI, but that's in keeping with similar outcomes for STEMI.

They do say that one thing that might partly explain this difference, which is an important point, is that more women may have non-obstructive coronary artery disease, meaning that there's something going on with the heart muscle, but they don't have blockage of a coronary vessel, which means that they're not having that ischemic event that's actually leading to or the cause of, quote, or I should say, which is by definition the heart attack.
The problem is, even if they don't technically have an NSTEMI, but instead have a non-obstructive coronary artery disease, they would still benefit from these treatments.
It's not a benign condition.

A lot of these therapies that you would give to somebody after a heart attack are the similar or the same therapies that you would give to somebody who's having non-obstructive coronary artery disease because they're preventive in nature as well.
And they're evidence-based and it's within the literature that they should be prescribed.

So even though some of the differences might be that women are more likely than men to present without a total blockage, they would still benefit from these evidence-based treatments, but they are not getting them.
And so that's the big outcome here.
Women by and large aren't getting as solid and as frequent evidence-based treatment as men when they come in.
And there's a lot of whys here.
There's a lot of this is like larger cultural whys having to do with how women have historically been treated within the healthcare system.
Sometimes their complaints are minimized.
Sometimes physicians think it's due to other things.
I think we've talked about this in the past.
It's a common type of bias that has to do with unconscious bias.
We see it a lot with like obesity shaming in our country where an individual might come into a hospital setting with a complaint that is in no way linked to their weight.
But the first thing a physician might think, well, it must have to do with their weight.
And we see this a lot with women, right?
A woman comes into the hospital complaining of something.
Does this have to do with your hormones?
You see it also a lot with trans individuals.
Oh, it must be because of the hormones that you're experiencing these symptoms, even when the symptoms aren't related to those issues.
And so that may partially explain what's going on, this sort of historical bias that we still haven't managed to move out of.
This difference between the rates of heart attack in women and men may partially explain why that bias persists.
But regardless of the fact that there's a bias that we're all working to overcome, the outcome is the same.
Women aren't getting as good of treatment post-heart attack as men.
And that's a problem that we have to correct.
Yeah.

I think a part of it, I mean, I think another factor here is what is the representativeness heuristic, which is something I talk a lot about to my residents and my students, et cetera, when I lecture about these kinds of things.
This is all just critical thinking in clinical decision making.

And one of the things that all people do, including physicians, is we fall for the representativeness heuristic in that we think something is likely to belong to a group or category if it has typical features of that category.
But that doesn't account for the base rate or statistics.
And part of what as educators, like as medical educators, we have to do is sort of teach our students to think differently than this naive thinking.
So one way to put it is that you don't really want to know how typical features are of a specific diagnosis.
You want to know how predictive they are of a specific diagnosis.
And it really, it's like a subtle difference, but it really can significantly change your thinking.
So part of the problem here is that the idea of what a typical heart attack patient is was developed 80 years ago or whatever, and was based upon a typical male heart attack.
And so we tend to think of a heart attack and the symptoms that look like a heart attack are the ones that men who are having a heart attack typically present with.
But they're different than the symptoms that women typically have, at least statistically speaking.
And so we're basically using a male algorithm on women and it doesn't work.
Which we do all the time in healthcare.
Which is a systemic problem in healthcare.
We're working on it.
And it's not like there's a lot of recognition of this and a lot of attempts at trying to fix this problem, but it's so deeply embedded it's going to take a long time to really weed it out.

And that's why these studies are being done to say, you know, there's still these male biased algorithms in our clinical decision making that's negatively impacting the care of women and we need to identify them and root them out.

And can I say it's so deeply embedded that this journal article, which was published in the Medical Journal of Australia, which was written by one, two, three, four women and two men, which I can only assume, I have not interviewed these individuals, but I can only assume that there was a curiosity within these researchers about this very issue, which drove them to do this research and publish.
Even these people in their first paragraph of the abstract, let me read this to you.

It's because it's so entrenched that the word typical in this context literally applies to men's symptoms.
Yeah, the males are typical and females are by definition atypical.
Yeah, although in their defense though, in their defense.
It's a medical term.
It is.
That's what every, they're communicating to physicians and that's what physicians would understand as typical versus atypical.
But it's interesting that they don't bracket that.
Yeah.
They could have meta-analyzed it and said, hey, by the way, we're calling them typical because that's how people understand it, but that is a part of the problem in and of itself.
It's part of the problem.
Yeah.
Yeah.
It's absolutely interesting.
Again, at the end of the day, you have a physician sitting in front of a patient and they have to figure out what's going on.
And all of these things come into play.

You have to calibrate to the specific patient, their history, their risk factors, how they would typically present with disease and also how they're expressing their symptoms and trying to figure out what that means.
But you always give, you always err on the side of making sure you're covering the things that you need to cover.
And the truth is those biases are so pervasive that we, like we women ourselves have them.

I would probably be less likely to think I was having a heart attack than a man, you know, let's say I'm 48 years old, I'm type A, I work really hard and I'm having some like jaw pain and maybe some left arm pain and some sense of like some really intense what I would consider like heartburn in my chest.
I might think it's something else.

Because it's normalized, right?

Plus we have a, we're very bad naively at statistics.

Oh, you're so right.
